Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $f:M\to N$ be smooth. Then there exist an open ball
$$ B\subseteq\mathbb R^m $$
containing $0$ and a smooth family of maps
$$ \mathcal F:M\times B\to N $$
such that $\mathcal F_0=f$ and, for every $p\in M$, the parameter map
$$ \mathcal F_p:B\to N,\qquad a\longmapsto \mathcal F(p,a), $$
is a submersion. In particular, the evaluation map $\mathcal F$ is a
submersion, so it is transverse to every closed embedded submanifold
$Z\subseteq N$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $A$ be a closed subset of a smooth manifold $M$, and let $U\subseteq M$ be open with $A\subseteq U$. Then there exists a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that $f=1$ on an open neighbourhood of $A$ and $\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq U$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

derivations.claim: Choose an open set $G\subset S$ on which all the required transverse conditions hold and containing the compact set $S\cap Z$. Inside $G$ choose a compact neighborhood $A$ of that intersection, by finitely many smaller coordinate disks; when the intersection is empty take $A=\varnothing$. By [F3] choose a smooth $\tau:S\to[0,1]$ equal to one near $S\setminus G$ and supported in $S\setminus A$. Replace it by its square if necessary. It vanishes near $A$, satisfies $d\tau=0$ wherever $\tau=0$, and every zero lies in $G$. Its support is compact and misses $Z$ as an ambient subset of $S$.

Apply [F1] to the inclusion $i:S\hookrightarrow S^3$, writing its family as $\mathcal F(p,a)$ with $\mathcal F(p,0)=i(p)$. Put $G_a(p)=\mathcal F(p,\tau(p)a)$ for parameters in a sufficiently small ball about zero. Where $\tau>0$ the parameter derivative is surjective. Where $\tau=0$ we have $G_a=i$ and source derivative $di$, because $d\tau=0$; the inclusion is transverse to every $T_i$ there by step 1.1. Thus the evaluation family is transverse to every target. By [F2] a finite union of null parameter sets contains all bad slices. Every small open parameter ball has positive measure, so there is a good parameter arbitrarily close to zero.

Choose the parameter small enough that every $G_{ta}$, $0\le t\le1$, is an embedding and their moving track stays disjoint from $Z$. Here embedding stability follows directly from compactness: finitely many graph charts for $i$ have projected derivatives bounded below on smaller convex charts, preserving local injectivity and immersion under a small $C^1$ perturbation; source pairs outside a common small chart distance have a positive minimum image separation, preserving global injectivity under a small $C^0$ perturbation. The compact set $i(\operatorname{supp}\tau)$ misses closed $Z$, so sufficiently small perturbations of it stay separated from $Z$. Smooth dependence on $a$ gives uniform $C^1$ smallness for the whole segment $ta$. The resulting isotopy is stationary outside $\operatorname{supp}\tau$ and can have any prescribed $C^1$ smallness.

Extend this embedding isotopy to an ambient isotopy $H_t$ by [F4], and let $Y_t=(\partial_tH_t)\circ H_t^{-1}$ be its velocity field. On each moving surface it agrees with $\partial_tG_{ta}$. Let $M$ be the compact track of $\operatorname{supp}\tau$; step 3.1 gives $M\cap Z=\varnothing$. By [F3] choose a smooth cutoff $\eta$ equal to one near $M$ with support disjoint from $Z$. Replace $Y_t$ by $X_t=\eta Y_t$ and take its flow using [F5]. At points of $G_{ta}(S)$ this field still equals the prescribed velocity: on the support track $\eta=1$, and outside it that velocity was zero. By uniqueness the new flow therefore extends the same surface isotopy. Its field vanishes on a neighborhood of $Z$, since its compact support misses $Z$, so it fixes that neighborhood pointwise.

The final slice is transverse to every target by the good-parameter choice in step 2.1, the protected neighborhood is fixed by step 4.1, and the surface isotopy has the arbitrarily prescribed $C^1$ smallness of step 3.1. If $m=0$ or $S$ is empty the identity isotopy already suffices, also consistent with the construction.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 treats an empty target family or empty surface by the identity.
Steps 1.1–4.1 allow an empty protected set or an empty moving support.

boundaries.reason: Smooth embedded targets and transverse protected patches exclude degenerate intersections.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 4.1 fix a neighborhood of the protected closed set.
Step 2.1 selects a parameter outside a finite union of null sets in a nonempty ball.

A **2-tangle diagram** is a regular diagram in a disk of two properly embedded tangle arcs and possibly finitely many closed tangle components, with four specified endpoints on the disk boundary; the arcs and circles are disjoint in the represented 3-ball, while their projections may have crossings. A **flyping circle** is a simple closed curve in the projection sphere whose intersection with the diagram consists of exactly three points, exactly one of which is a crossing; the circle is transverse to both branches at that crossing and to the diagram at the other two points. A small annular neighborhood of this circle has two complementary tangle disks. A **flype** fixes the tangle in one disk, interchanges which pair of strands crosses in the annular neighborhood, and turns over the tangle in the other disk: its projected tangle is reflected and all its over-under crossing data are reversed. This turnover is a half-turn in three-dimensional space about an axis in the projection sphere. Component orientations are transported by this motion, and the exterior diagram is fixed. The move with the opposite choice of fixed disk is also allowed; a disk containing no crossings is allowed. A flype whose fixed tangle has no crossings is called an **entire flype**. Diagrams are drawn on the oriented projection sphere; a **sphere planar isotopy** is an orientation-preserving smooth isotopy of that sphere carrying the decorated diagram. A plane diagram is obtained by choosing a point of the sphere outside the projection and deleting it. At each crossing of a link diagram, a **crossing ball** is a small 3-ball in which the overpass lies on the upper hemisphere and the underpass lies on the lower hemisphere, with the rest of the link outside that ball. Replacing all crossing disks by upper hemispheres or by lower hemispheres gives the shifted projection spheres $S_+$ and $S_-$. A **saddle disk** in a crossing ball is a properly embedded disk whose boundary meets each of the two hemispheres in two arcs and whose interior passes across the equatorial crossing disk. For a closed embedded surface transverse to the link and to $S_+$ and $S_-$, each component $C$ of its intersection with either shifted sphere has a **bubble word**: read once around $C$, recording $P$ each time it crosses the link and $S$ each time it passes through a crossing ball along a saddle disk. The surface is in **bubble standard position** if every such word is nonempty and no word records the same crossing ball more than once. A **Conway sphere** is an embedded sphere meeting the link transversely in four points; it is in crossing-ball standard position when its intersection with the crossing balls consists of saddle disks and its shifted-sphere intersection curves satisfy the bubble-standard conditions.

The turnover convention is the one in Kindred's Definition 2.9 and Figure 1. In particular, an entire flype permits viewing the whole diagram from the opposite side of the sphere, as in his Definition 2.11. Closed components inside a tangle disk are carried along with its arcs.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a smooth link and $S\subset S^3$ a smooth closed embedded surface. Supply finitely many pairwise disjoint closed smooth balls $C_j$, each with coordinates extending to a neighborhood and identifying $C_j$ with the closed unit ball. Require that the whole intersection $L\cap C_j$ consists of the upper overpass $\{y=0,x^2+z^2=1,z\ge0\}$ and lower underpass $\{x=0,y^2+z^2=1,z\le0\}$ in these coordinates, and that $S\cap L\cap C_j=\varnothing$.

For every open neighborhood $W$ of $\bigcup_j C_j$, there is a smooth ambient isotopy of $S^3$, fixing $L$ pointwise and equal to the identity outside $W$, whose final surface meets each $C_j$ in a finite, possibly empty, disjoint collection of the quadrilateral saddle disks of the explicit crossing-ball foliation. In particular the final surface is transverse to each $\partial C_j$, each saddle boundary has four equatorial corners and two arcs on each hemisphere, and all disks in one ball are ordered levels of one smooth foliation. The isotopy fixes a neighborhood of $S\cap L$. This assertion does not impose the disk-piece or repeated-bubble conditions on the parts outside the crossing balls.

Let $C=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2+z^2\le1\}$, with upper overpass $A_+=\{y=0,x^2+z^2=1,z\ge0\}$ and lower underpass $A_-=\{x=0,y^2+z^2=1,z\le0\}$. For every compact $K\subset C\setminus(A_+\cup A_-)$ there are $0<a<b<1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ such that, on a neighborhood of $C$, the smooth function
$$q(x,y,z)=\frac{z+x^2-y^2}{d(z)},\qquad d(z)=1+\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-\varepsilon-z^2$$
has these properties:

1. $K\subset\{|q|<a\}$, $q\ge1$ on $A_+$ and $q\le-1$ on $A_-$.
2. For each $|h|\le b$, $D_h=C\cap q^{-1}(h)$ is a smooth proper disk transverse to $\partial C$. Projection to the $(x,y)$-plane identifies it with a smooth star-shaped disk. Its boundary meets $z=0$ in exactly four points, one in each open quadrant; its intersections with each open hemisphere are two arcs. The disks are disjoint and strictly ordered by height above every common projected point.
3. On $C\cap\{|q|\le b\}$ there is a smooth vector field $V$ tangent to the levels of $q$, with $(V_x,V_y)=(x,y)$, zero exactly on the vertical axis, and pointing strictly outward on $\partial C\cap\{|q|\le b\}$. Consequently radial dilation in these level coordinates is compatible with the boundary of the crossing ball.

This supplies the local foliation and vector field, not an ambient positioning theorem for a surface.

Assume countable choice. Let $S$ be a compact smooth embedded surface without boundary in $S^3$, let $Z\subset S^3$ be closed, and let $T_1,\ldots,T_m$ be finitely many closed smooth embedded surfaces. Suppose $S$ is transverse to every $T_i$ on a neighborhood in $S$ of $S\cap Z$. Then there is a smooth ambient isotopy fixing a neighborhood of $Z$ pointwise whose final surface is transverse to every $T_i$. The induced isotopy of embeddings of $S$ may be taken arbitrarily close to the inclusion in the $C^1$ topology.

Thus protected surface patches and protected link points are unchanged when their original intersections with the target surfaces are already transverse. No transversality is asserted at a protected nontransverse intersection.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Assume countable choice. Let $B$ be a supplied smooth closed $3$-ball and let $F\subset B$ be a compact neatly properly embedded smooth surface, possibly disconnected, with no closed components. If at least one component of $F$ is not a disk, there exists an embedded disk $X\subset\operatorname{int}B$ such that $X\cap F=\partial X$ and $\partial X$ does not bound a disk in $F$. The assertion concerns a geometric compressing disk for the whole surface; it does not require specifying its boundary component in advance.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a nonsplit smooth link and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smooth sphere meeting $L$ transversely in two points. Let $D$ be an embedded disk with $\partial D=c\subset S\setminus L$ and $\operatorname{int}D\cap(S\cup L)=\varnothing$. Assume the disk meets $S$ transversely along its boundary collar.

Then $c$ bounds a disk $E\subset S\setminus L$. Replacing $E$ by $D$, with a small collar push and corner rounding near $c$, gives a sphere $S'$ ambient isotopic to $S$ by an isotopy fixing $L$ pointwise. The endpoint sphere agrees with $S$ outside $E$ and an arbitrarily small collar of $c$, and its new disk lies in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of $D$. In particular the two punctures and the nontriviality of either side tangle are preserved.

Assume countable choice. Let $H$ be a smooth closed disk on a smooth sphere $P$, and let $I_0,I_1$ be disjoint open intervals on $\partial H$ with disjoint closures. Let $\Gamma$ be a finite disjoint collection of smooth embedded circles on $P$, transverse to $\partial H$. Suppose $\Gamma\cap H$ consists of finitely many proper arcs, each joining $I_0$ to $I_1$. If some circle of $\Gamma$ meets $H$ in at least two arcs, then some circle $C\in\Gamma$ has two arcs $\alpha_0,\alpha_1\subset H$ bounding a closed rectangle $R\subset H$ with its other two sides subintervals of $I_0,I_1$, and
$$\operatorname{int}_H(R)\cap\Gamma=\varnothing.$$
Here the rectangle's interior means its two-dimensional interior in $H$. Moreover $C$ bounds a disk $D\subset P$ containing $R$, and $R\cap C=\alpha_0\cup\alpha_1$. The chosen circle need not be the originally supplied repeated circle.

Assume countable choice. Let $L$ be a nonsplit smooth link and let $S$ be a smooth sphere meeting $L$ transversely twice. Supply pairwise disjoint closed crossing balls $C_1,\ldots,C_n$ such that $S\cap C_j$ is a finite collection of proper saddle disks disjoint from $L$. Supply also a closed ball $B$ whose interior misses $L$ and every $C_j$, such that $S\cap B$ is a finite neat proper disk family.

In one crossing ball $C=C_k$, let $\sigma_0,\sigma_1$ be two adjacent saddle disks: their boundary circles cobound an annulus $A\subset\partial C$ with interior disjoint from $S\cup L$. Suppose a rectangle $R\subset A\cap\partial B$ joins an arc $\alpha_0\subset\partial\sigma_0$ to an arc $\alpha_1\subset\partial\sigma_1$, its other sides span the annulus, and $R\cap S=\alpha_0\cup\alpha_1$. Require that $R$ misses $L$, and that these two arcs lie on the boundary of the same disk component $E$ of $S\cap B$. All shared faces and their surface pieces have supplied compatible corner roundings.

Then there is an ambient isotopy fixing $L$ pointwise whose final sphere agrees with $S$ near every other saddle disk and meets each crossing ball in precisely its old saddle disks with $\sigma_0,\sigma_1$ deleted from $C_k$. In particular its total number of saddle disks decreases by exactly two. This is the overpass-free rectangle case; no meridional-surgery case is included.

Assume countable choice. Let a sphere $S$ meet a smooth link $L$ transversely twice, with both side tangles nontrivial. Supply finitely many pairwise disjoint closed coordinate crossing balls $C_j$, disjoint from the two punctures, such that $S\cap C_j$ is a finite collection of ordered disks in one explicit quadrilateral saddle foliation for each ball. Suppose a ball $B$ has interior disjoint from $L$ and every crossing ball, and $S\cap B$ is a finite neat proper disk family.

In one crossing ball $C_k$, assume all the uppermost-saddle rectangle hypotheses of the meridional-disk lemma: both upper arcs of its largest-level saddle $\sigma$ belong to one disk component of $S\cap B$, their central upper-hemisphere rectangle contains the overpass and has interior disjoint from $S$, and the two crossing arcs have the specified semicircle coordinates. All shared faces have compatible corner roundings.

Then meridional surgery followed by an ambient isotopy preserving $L$ setwise gives a two-point sphere $S'$ with both side tangles nontrivial, whose punctures lie outside all the crossing balls, and whose intersection with each crossing ball consists of a subset of the original whole saddle disks, with $\sigma$ excluded. In particular, if $s(S)=\sum_j\#\pi_0(S\cap C_j)$, then $s(S')\le s(S)-1$. The post-surgery isotopy need not fix the punctures pointwise.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $A$ be a closed subset of a smooth manifold $M$, and let $U\subseteq M$ be open with $A\subseteq U$. Then there exists a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that $f=1$ on an open neighbourhood of $A$ and $\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq U$.

derivations.claim: First move the two punctures of the supplied sphere onto link edges outside all crossing balls. Each link component has an open subarc there: inside the disjoint crossing balls its pieces are only arcs with distinct endpoints, so a whole closed component cannot be contained in their union. On each component containing punctures, choose distinct target points in such a subarc with the same cyclic order. There is a smooth increasing circle diffeomorphism taking the old points to the new ones. To construct it, choose a positive smooth periodic derivative with prescribed integrals on the finitely many intervening intervals: start with a sufficiently small positive constant and add positive interior bumps to obtain each required positive target interval length. Integrate, fixing one initial value. Interpolation of its increasing lift with the identity is a smooth circle isotopy. Extend its velocity off the link in finitely many link-axis charts, patch with smooth cutoffs, and set it to zero on other components. By [F9] its ambient flow preserves $L$ setwise and realizes the circle isotopy. Transporting the sphere preserves nontriviality of both side tangles and places its punctures outside the crossing balls.

Apply [F2] to obtain a sphere with finite saddle position, and fix the resulting explicit foliation function $q_j$ in each crossing ball for the rest of the argument. Make the sphere transverse to both $S_+,S_-$ using [F3] with protected set $L\cup\bigcup_jC_j$. The required transversality already holds near that protected intersection: proper foliation disks meet both hemispheres transversely, their four equatorial corners are simple, and the compatible roundings retain these transverse charts. Explicitly at a corner $x,y\ne0$ the level normal is $(2x,-2y,1)$; it cannot be parallel to any combination of the equatorial normal $(0,0,1)$ and the hemisphere normal $(x,y,0)$, since the two nonzero horizontal coordinates would require opposite proportionality factors. Thus the usual collar rounding also preserves the transverse condition. At a link puncture outside the crossing balls, transversality to $L\subset P$ forces transversality to $P$: a surface tangent to $P$ would contain the link tangent and fail to be transverse to the link. Thus [F3] applies and preserves all fixed foliation patches. The class $\mathcal A$ of nontrivial two-point spheres with punctures outside the crossing balls, transverse to both shifted spheres and meeting each crossing ball in a finite subset of levels of its fixed $q_j$, is nonempty.

For $T\in\mathcal A$ put $s(T)=\sum_j\#\pi_0(T\cap C_j)$ and $c(T)=\#\pi_0(T\cap S_+)+\#\pi_0(T\cap S_-)$. These are finite natural numbers, the second by compact transverse one-manifold intersections. Use [F4] first to minimize $s$ over $\mathcal A$, and then to minimize $c$ among spheres attaining that least $s$. Choose a sphere attaining both minima. This is a global minimum over all such nontrivial decomposing spheres; it is not restricted to the isotopy class of the starting sphere. Hence a nontrivial meridional child in $\mathcal A$ is an admissible competitor.

Every component of $T\cap B_\pm$ has boundary. A closed component would be open and closed in the connected sphere and equal to $T$, contrary to its punctures on the boundary link and transversality there. If a component on one side were not a disk, [F5] would supply a compression disk $D$ in that ball interior, missing the whole surface, the link and every crossing ball. Its boundary bounds a puncture-free disk $E$ on $T$. This disk contains at least one shifted-sphere cut circle: otherwise it would lie wholly in the original ball piece and contradict the essentiality of the compression boundary. Since $\partial E$ misses all crossing balls and both shifted spheres, $E$ contains whole saddle patches and whole cut circles whenever it meets their interiors. Replacing $E$ by $D$ therefore deletes some whole saddles and at least one cut circle, and adds none; the new patch and boundary collar lie in the open-side ball. The retained surface remains transverse to both shifted spheres and retains only original fixed foliation levels. Nontriviality is preserved by the link-fixed isotopy in [F5], so this is a sphere in $\mathcal A$ with smaller $(s,c)$, a contradiction. Both side pieces are consequently disks.

Suppose a shifted-sphere intersection circle has empty bubble word. It lies in the common projection face, avoids the link and every hemisphere, and is therefore the same intersection circle on $S_+$ and $S_-$. Its incident upper and lower pieces are disks by step 4.1, each with this as its sole boundary. Their union is a closed component of $T$: the surface crosses the common face transversely, so these are its two local sides along the circle, with no further sheet attached. The union is both open and closed in connected $T$, hence is all of $T$. But it misses $L$, since the two disk interiors lie in the link-free ball interiors and their common boundary has no puncture. This contradicts the two link intersections. Thus all bubble words are nonempty.

Suppose an upper shifted-sphere circle meets one hemisphere more than once. The finitely many upper saddle arcs span two disjoint equatorial intervals, chosen on the $x>0$ and $x<0$ sides to contain their finitely many endpoints. Apply [F6] to obtain an empty rectangle $R$ between two arcs of one intersection circle. That circle bounds one of the disk pieces $E$ from step 4.1. The upper arcs have the order: the positive-$y$ arcs in increasing saddle height, followed by the negative-$y$ arcs in decreasing height. This follows from the four corner equations $x^2=(1+h)/2$, $y^2=(1-h)/2$ and the disjointness of the foliation levels in [F2]. Thus if $R$ misses the overpass its two arcs are of the same type and belong to distinct adjacent saddle levels. If $R$ meets the overpass, its interior contains the whole overpass except its endpoints, since no saddle arc meets that connected overpass. Emptiness then forces its two arc sides to be the positive-$y$ and negative-$y$ arcs of the same uppermost saddle. These are the only two possibilities.

In the overpass-free case the annulus between the two adjacent saddle boundaries is the boundary level band between their parameters: the boundary restriction of $q_j$ is a submersion there with one circle per level. It misses $T$ in its interior and misses $L$, because all link arcs have $|q_j|\ge1$ outside the middle foliation band. The rectangle spans this annulus and its two sides lie on the one disk piece $E$. Apply [F7] to delete the two saddle patches, preserving nontriviality of both tangles. If necessary restore simultaneous transversality outside the protected balls using [F3], again fixing the link and every crossing ball. The remaining saddle levels are unchanged, so the new sphere lies in $\mathcal A$ and has $s$ smaller by two. This contradicts step 3.1.

In the central-rectangle case apply [F8]. It produces a sphere with both side tangles nontrivial, punctures outside the crossing balls, and only a subset of the original saddle levels, with the uppermost saddle absent. Restore exterior simultaneous transversality with [F3], if needed, preserving all remaining patches. This gives a member of $\mathcal A$ with strictly smaller $s$, again contradicting step 3.1. Consequently no upper intersection circle repeats a bubble. For the lower sphere use the coordinate change $(x,y,z)\mapsto(y,x,-z)$ in each ball. It exchanges overpass and underpass and sends $q_j$ to $-q_j$, so the identical two cases and their exact decreases apply with the signs reversed. No lower intersection circle repeats a bubble either.

The minimizing sphere retains both nontrivial side tangles and two punctures outside the crossing balls by its membership in $\mathcal A$. Step 4.1 gives disk pieces, step 5.1 gives nonempty words, and steps 6.1–6.2 exclude repeated bubbles on either shifted sphere. By [F1] these are exactly the stated bubble-standard conditions. The global minimization explicitly allowed replacement by a nontrivial meridional child, so no unproved isotopy claim about the original decomposing sphere has been used.

Steps 6.1–6.2 include one uppermost saddle and a child with zero saddles.
